course: Fortified Corn-Soy Porridge for Malnourished Children

lessons.title: Cleaning corn and soybeans by winnowing and washing
lessons.body:
Start by spreading your corn and soybeans on a clean tarpaulin or woven mat in the sun. Pick out stones, dirt clods, insects, and any mouldy or discoloured grains. Mouldy grains are dangerousâthey can contain poisons that survive cooking. For 10 kg of corn, you should spend at least 15 minutes hand-sorting. Do the same for soybeans: remove shrivelled, green, or black beans.

Next, winnow to remove lighter chaff and dust. On a windy day, pour the grains slowly from one basin to another from a height of about 1 metre. The wind blows away husks and dust while heavier grains fall into the lower basin. If there is no wind, use a fan or gently blow with your mouth. Repeat 3â4 times until no chaff remains.

Washing removes remaining dirt and some surface germs. Put grains in a large basin, cover with clean water, and rub them between your hands for 2â3 minutes. The water will turn cloudy. Pour off the dirty water and repeat with fresh water until the water stays clearâusually 3 rinses. For soybeans, soaking is not needed for this porridge, but washing is essential because soybeans often carry soil bacteria.

After washing, drain the grains in a colander or sieve. Spread them on a clean mat or tray to dry in the sun for 2â4 hours, or until they are dry to the touch. Wet grains will stick together during roasting and can grow mould. If you are processing 20 kg, split the work into smaller batches of 5 kg so that every grain is properly cleaned. Always wash your hands and use clean toolsâdirty hands can recontaminate the grains. Clean grains are the foundation of safe, healthy porridge.

lessons.title: Roasting soybeans to remove beany taste and anti-nutrients
lessons.body:
Raw soybeans contain anti-nutrients like trypsin inhibitor that block protein digestion and cause stomach upset. Roasting destroys these anti-nutrients and removes the strong beany taste that children dislike. You will need a dry frying pan, a large pot, or a clay pot. A metal pan heats faster, but stir constantly to avoid burning.

Measure your cleaned, dried soybeans. For a standard batch, use 2 kg of soybeans. Heat your pan over medium fireânot high, because high heat burns the outside while the inside stays raw. When a drop of water sizzles and disappears immediately, the pan is ready. Add the soybeans in a single layer, about 2â3 cm deep. Do not overcrowd; if you have more, roast in batches.

Stir continuously with a wooden spoon or paddle for 15â20 minutes. The beans will first crackle, then darken to a golden brown. You will see small brown spots and smell a nutty aroma. That is the sign they are done. If you see black spots or smoke, the heat is too highâreduce the fire and keep stirring. Raw soybeans are hard; roasted ones are brittle and easy to break between your teeth.

After roasting, spread the beans on a clean tray to cool for 10â15 minutes. They must be completely cool before milling, or they will clog the mill. Roasted soybeans can be stored in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks in a dry place. Always roast soybeans separately from corn because they need different times and temperatures. Properly roasted soybeans are safe, digestible, and give the porridge a rich, nutty flavour that masks the beany taste. Never skip this stepâit is critical for child health.

lessons.title: Roasting corn for better flavor and digestibility
lessons.body:
Roasting corn improves its flavour, makes it easier to digest, and reduces cooking time later. You will need whole dried corn kernelsânot fresh corn. Clean and dry them as you learned in Lesson 1. Use a large dry pan, pot, or a traditional clay baking pot. A wide pan gives more surface area and roasts faster.

Measure 3 kg of dried corn. Heat your pan over medium fire. Test the heat by sprinkling a few drops of waterâthey should sizzle and evaporate in 2 seconds. Add the corn in a layer no deeper than 3 cm. Stir constantly with a wooden spoon. The corn will start to pop slightly and turn a deeper yellow. After 10â12 minutes, you will see light brown patches. Keep stirring for another 5â8 minutes until most kernels are golden brown and smell like roasted maize. Total roasting time is 15â20 minutes.

Do not let the corn turn black or dark brownâthat means burnt, and it will make the porridge bitter. If you hear loud popping, that is normal, but reduce heat slightly. Burnt corn can also form harmful compounds. When done, pour the corn onto a clean mat or tray to cool completely. It should be cool to the touch before milling, about 20â30 minutes.

Roasted corn is lighter and crushes more easily than raw corn. It also has a sweeter, nuttier taste that children prefer. Store roasted corn in a dry sack or airtight container for up to 1 month. Always roast in a well-ventilated areaâsmoke from roasting can irritate your eyes and lungs. If you are roasting both corn and soybeans, do corn first, then soybeans, because soybeans leave an oily residue that can burn. With practice, you will know the right colour and smell by heart.

lessons.title: Using a local mill to grind corn and soybeans into flour
lessons.body:
After roasting and cooling, you need to grind the corn and soybeans into fine flour. You can use a local hammer mill, a disc mill, or a traditional grinding stone. Most African villages have a mill that charges a small fee per kilogramâoften 500â1000 shillings or 0.50â1 USD per 10 kg. Call ahead to make sure the mill is clean and not used for other products like fish or spices, which can leave smells.

Before milling, mix your roasted corn and roasted soybeans in the correct ratio. For a standard fortified porridge, use 70% corn and 30% soybeans by weight. For example, for 10 kg of flour, use 7 kg roasted corn and 3 kg roasted soybeans. Mix them well in a basin so that every scoop has both grains. This ensures each serving has balanced protein and energy.

Take your mixture to the mill. Ask the miller to set the grinder to a fine settingâlike for maize meal, not coarse like for animal feed. Feed the grains slowly into the hopper. If the mill is too fast, the flour will be hot and may clog. You may need to pass the flour through the mill twice to get a fine texture. The first pass breaks the grains; the second makes it powdery. For 10 kg, milling takes about 10â15 minutes.

Collect the flour in a clean, dry sack or bucket. Do not use a sack that previously held chemicals or dirty produce. Immediately after milling, spread the flour on a clean tray to cool for 10 minutesâmilling generates heat. Then pack it into airtight containers or double plastic bags. Label with the date. Freshly milled flour should be used within 2â3 months. If you cannot mill immediately, store the roasted grains in a dry place for up to 2 weeks. Never grind wet grainsâthey will ruin the mill and spoil the flour.

lessons.title: Sieving flour to get the right texture for porridge
lessons.body:
Sieving removes coarse particles, hulls, and any lumps from your milled flour. The right texture is important: too coarse and the porridge will be gritty and hard for a sick child to swallow; too fine and it may become gluey. You will need a fine-mesh sieve or a traditional woven sieve. A 1 mm mesh is idealâabout the size of a mosquito net.

Place your sieve over a large clean basin. Add flour a few cups at a time. Shake the sieve gently side to side, or tap it with your hand. Do not press the flour through with your fingersâthat forces coarse bits through. The fine flour falls into the basin; the coarse bits stay in the sieve. For 10 kg of milled flour, sieving takes about 20â30 minutes. Work in a clean, draft-free area so dust does not blow away.

What to do with the coarse bits? You can re-mill them, or if you have no mill, you can use them for animal feed or compost. Do not throw them into the porridgeâthey will not cook soft and can cause choking. The sieved fine flour should be soft like baby powder. Test by rubbing a pinch between your fingers: it should feel smooth, not sandy.

After sieving, you may want to blend different batches to ensure consistency. Mix the sieved flour well with a clean spoon. Then pack immediately into airtight containers. Sieving also helps remove any small stones or metal bits that might have come from the millâalways check the sieve for foreign objects. If you are making porridge for a malnourished child, the flour must be fine enough to cook into a smooth, drinkable liquid. A good test: mix 2 tablespoons of flour with 1 cup of waterâit should form a smooth paste with no lumps. If lumps form, sieve again or blend in a dry mill. Proper sieving makes the porridge smooth, digestible, and safe.

lessons.title: Preventing contamination during milling and packaging
lessons.body:
Contamination can happen at any stepâfrom dirty hands to unclean mills to poor storage. Your goal is to keep the flour free from dirt, germs, insects, and chemicals. Start with personal hygiene: wash your hands with soap and water before handling grains or flour. Wear a clean apron and tie back long hair. Do not smoke, eat, or chew while working.

At the mill, check that the equipment is clean. Ask the miller to run a small handful of your grain through first and throw it awayâthis cleans out old flour from previous customers. If the mill was used for peanuts, fish, or spices, the smell can transfer to your flour. In that case, find another mill or clean the mill with a dry cloth and run a batch of plain corn through it first. Never use a mill that has milled poisonous seeds like castor beansâtraces can be deadly.

During milling, keep your collection sack or bucket clean and off the ground. Place it on a clean mat or table. Do not let the flour touch the floor, which may have animal droppings or chemicals. After milling, cool the flour completely before packaging. Hot flour creates condensation inside the container, which leads to mould. Use food-grade plastic bags, clean jerrycans, or airtight buckets. Double-bagging is best: put flour in a small bag, twist it closed, then place it in a larger bag.

For packaging, work on a clean table. Use a scoop that is only for flourânot for chemicals or animal feed. Fill bags to the top, press out air, and seal tightly with a knot or heat sealer. Label each bag with the date and contents. Store in a cool, dry, dark place off the floor, like on a shelf or pallet. Keep away from soap, kerosene, or pesticides. Check weekly for insects or moisture. If you see clumps or smell mould, throw the flour awayâdo not feed it to children. Clean tools and careful storage protect the health of the children you are feeding.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove mouldy grains before processing?
options: B) They can contain poisons that survive cooking
C) They are harder to mill
D) They make the flour darker
quiz.explanation: Mouldy grains can contain mycotoxins that are harmful even after cooking.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of winnowing?
options: B) To remove chaff and dust
quiz.explanation: Winnowing uses wind to blow away lighter chaff and dust from the grains.

quiz.q: How many times should you rinse grains until the water stays clear?
quiz.explanation: Usually 3 rinses are needed until the water runs clear.

quiz.q: Why must grains be dried after washing before roasting?
options: B) To prevent sticking and mould
quiz.explanation: Wet grains stick together during roasting and can grow mould.

quiz.q: What is a sign that the pan is ready for roasting soybeans?
options: B) A drop of water sizzles and disappears
quiz.explanation: A water drop sizzling and disappearing immediately indicates the pan is hot enough.

quiz.q: How long should you roast soybeans?
quiz.explanation: Roasting soybeans takes about 15â20 minutes with constant stirring.

quiz.q: What anti-nutrient in raw soybeans is destroyed by roasting?
quiz.explanation: Trypsin inhibitor blocks protein digestion and is destroyed by heat.

quiz.q: Why should you not overcrowd the pan when roasting soybeans?
quiz.explanation: Overcrowding leads to uneven roastingâsome beans burn while others stay raw.

quiz.q: What colour should roasted soybeans be?
quiz.explanation: Golden brown with a nutty aroma indicates properly roasted soybeans.

quiz.q: Why roast corn?
options: B) For better flavour and digestibility
quiz.explanation: Roasting improves flavour, digestibility, and reduces cooking time.

quiz.q: How deep should the corn layer be in the pan?
quiz.explanation: A layer no deeper than 3 cm allows even roasting.

quiz.q: What should you do if the corn starts to pop loudly?
quiz.explanation: Loud popping means the heat is high; reducing it prevents burning.

quiz.q: How long should roasted corn cool before milling?
options: D) It doesn't need to cool
quiz.explanation: Corn must be completely cool to the touch before milling.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio of corn to soybeans for fortified porridge?
quiz.explanation: A 70:30 ratio provides balanced protein and energy.

quiz.q: Why should you mix corn and soybeans before milling?
options: B) To ensure each serving has balanced nutrients
quiz.explanation: Mixing ensures every scoop of flour has both grains for consistent nutrition.

quiz.q: What mill setting should you use for porridge flour?
quiz.explanation: A fine setting produces smooth flour suitable for porridge.

quiz.q: Why might you need to pass the flour through the mill twice?
options: B) To get a finer texture
quiz.explanation: A second pass breaks down coarse particles for a finer flour.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after milling?
options: D) Store in a sack on the floor
quiz.explanation: Flour must cool completely before packaging to prevent condensation and mould.

quiz.q: How long can freshly milled flour be stored?
quiz.explanation: Properly stored flour should be used within 2â3 months.

quiz.q: What is the ideal mesh size for sieving porridge flour?
quiz.explanation: A 1 mm mesh removes coarse particles while keeping fine flour.

quiz.q: How should you push flour through the sieve?
options: C) Use a spoon to force it
quiz.explanation: Gentle shaking allows fine flour to fall through without forcing coarse bits.

quiz.q: What can you do with the coarse bits left in the sieve?
options: B) Re-mill or use for animal feed
quiz.explanation: Coarse bits can be re-milled or used for animal feed or compost.

quiz.q: How can you test if sieved flour is fine enough?
options: B) Rub a pinch between fingers
quiz.explanation: Rubbing a pinch should feel smooth, not sandy.

quiz.q: Why is sieving important for malnourished children?
options: B) It ensures smooth, digestible texture
quiz.explanation: Fine flour cooks into a smooth liquid that is easy for weak children to swallow.

quiz.q: What should you do before handling grains or flour?
quiz.explanation: Washing hands with soap prevents contamination.

quiz.q: Why should you run a small batch of your grain through the mill first?
options: B) To clean out old flour
quiz.explanation: This removes leftover flour from previous customers, reducing contamination.

quiz.q: What type of mill should you avoid?
options: C) One that milled poisonous seeds
quiz.explanation: Mills that processed poisonous seeds like castor beans can leave deadly traces.

quiz.q: Why should you not package hot flour?
options: B) It creates condensation and mould
quiz.explanation: Hot flour releases moisture that condenses inside the container, leading to mould.

quiz.q: How should you store packaged flour?
options: B) In a cool, dry, dark place off the floor
quiz.explanation: A cool, dry, dark place off the floor protects flour from moisture, pests, and chemicals.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see clumps or smell mould in stored flour?
quiz.explanation: Mouldy flour can be toxic and should never be fed to children.
